title: The Implicit Bias of Hyperbolic Representation Learning for Multiclass Data: A Busemann Risk Perspective
claim: Points and geodesics in curved space are described by the same geometry at large radius: rays reach ideal boundary points and horospheres give the level sets.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side; 3D hyperboloid left, 2D disk right; labeled callouts
description: Two-panel geometric illustration of hyperbolic space. Panel (a) shows a 3D hyperboloid as a cyan mesh surface inside a light-yellow cone with dashed asymptotes. Blue coordinate axes are marked with ±√K. A red curve on the hyperboloid is projected by black arrows from the point -√K down onto a flat Poincaré disk at the base, where a red curve also appears. Labels read Hyperboloid, Poincaré Disk and Ideal Boundary. Panel (b) is a top-down Poincaré disk with a grey-teal grid. It marks the origin o, a point x, and an ideal point ξ on the boundary ∂H^n. A cyan geodesic ray γ_ξ(t) runs to ξ, and green nested horospheres touch ξ. The eye goes first to the cone and the cyan lines.
caption: Geometric illustration of hyperbolic representations and their boundary asymptotics.
abstract: We study the implicit bias of Riemannian gradient flow for hyperbolic multiclass classification with fixed class prototypes in hyperbolic space $\mathbb H^n$. Our framework accommodates general permutation invariant relative margin (PERM) losses, a class that includes cross entropy and other standard multiclass losses. Our analysis is based on a decomposition: at large radius, the distance to each prototype splits into a radial term and a direction dependent term described by the Busemann function. This yields two main results. First, we prove a radial dichotomy: the sign of a drift coefficient $Î¼$ determines whether the radius is pushed toward the ideal boundary or back toward the interior; if the positive drift persists, then $r(t)=\tfrac12\log t+O(1)$, while persistent negative drift returns the trajectory to the large radius threshold in finite time. Second, we show that large-radius directions can approach critical points of the Busemann risk on $\partial\mathbb H^n$, even during radial return. These results provide a rigorous large-radius perspective on two phenomena we refer to as boundary saturation and near-boundary clustering in hyperbolic representation learning.
